Financial Statements: Balance Sheet, Income Statement, Depreciation, GAAP, Accounts Payable and Receivable

Unit 1: Financial Management. Lesson 4 of 60 in CHTM Academy.

You are invited to a leadership meeting where the finance officer walks through the hospital's statements before the capital list is discussed. Nobody will explain the terms to you. Your ten-million-dollar inventory is sitting inside one of those statements, and the way it is carried there decides how your replacement request is heard.

The two statements a manager must recognize

Statement            Covers            Lines                            Where equipment shows up
Balance sheet        one day           assets, liabilities, equity      an asset, at book value
Income statement     a period          revenue, expenses, net income    depreciation and service
                                                                        expense

The balance sheet is a snapshot on a single date, and it balances: assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity. Your equipment sits on the asset side at its book value. The income statement, also called the profit and loss statement, covers a period of a month, a quarter, or a full year: revenue minus expenses equals net income. Your department touches it through salaries, parts, contracts, and the depreciation of the assets you asked for.

Cash flow deserves one paragraph. The cash flow statement tracks money in and money out over a period, split into operating, investing, and financing. It exists because reported profit is not money in the bank. A hospital can show net income and still have no cash this quarter for your capital item, and that is a real answer rather than an excuse.

Depreciation, and why a fully depreciated device still runs

Depreciation spreads a capital item's cost across its useful life. Straight-line is the common method: (cost minus salvage value) / useful life, per year. A $1,000,000 system over a ten-year useful life with no salvage depreciates $100,000 a year. Book value = cost minus accumulated depreciation, so after three years that system is carried at $700,000.

Here is the trap. Book value is an accounting position, not a condition report. A device that is fully depreciated has a book value of zero and may still be accurate, safe, supported, and years from replacement. Another device may be half depreciated and already unsupportable. Replacement is argued on support, failure trend, parts availability, and clinical need, never on the depreciation schedule alone. The schedule matters in one direction only: disposing of an asset still being depreciated writes off the remaining book value, which is a hit finance must agree to in advance.

GAAP and why the department follows it

GAAP stands for generally accepted accounting principles: the standards, conventions, and rules accountants follow when they record transactions and prepare statements. A manager does not apply GAAP personally, but a manager lives inside it. It is why a part cannot be expensed in a convenient month, why capital and expense are not interchangeable, and why the auditor can ask to see the receiving document behind a number. Consistent rules are what make one year comparable with the next.

Payables, receivables, and business activity reports

Accounts payable is what the hospital owes its vendors, and your unpaid service invoices and parts orders sit there. Your part in it is real: you approve the invoice, confirm the work was done and documented, and withhold approval when the service report never arrived. Accounts receivable is what the hospital is owed, and it holds the revenue from any service your department sells outside, plus the chargebacks billed to clinical cost centers. A business activity report is the periodic summary of what the department did and what it cost, written for leadership: volumes, labor, cost by category, and the trend. It is how a non-financial department shows its work in financial language.

Exam tip: balance sheet is one day and holds assets, liabilities, and equity; income statement is a period and holds revenue, expenses, and net. Straight-line depreciation is (cost minus salvage) / useful life, and book value is cost minus accumulated depreciation. Payable is what the hospital owes; receivable is what it is owed. Fully depreciated never means unusable.
Remember
The balance sheet is a one-day snapshot of assets, liabilities, and equity, the income statement is a period of revenue, expenses, and net, and a device's book value is an accounting number that says nothing about its remaining useful life.
Deeper explanation

Financial Statements: Balance Sheet, Income Statement, Depreciation, GAAP, Accounts Payable and Receivable, explained slowly

A small balance sheet

This is a simplified hospital balance sheet on the last day of a fiscal year. It balances, because it must: assets equal liabilities plus equity.

ASSETS                                      LIABILITIES
Cash and short-term investments    42,000    Accounts payable            31,000
Accounts receivable, net           88,000    Accrued salaries and
Inventories and supplies           14,000      benefits                  19,000
Property, plant and equipment               Current portion of debt      12,000
  Land and buildings              310,000    Long-term debt             186,000
  Medical equipment, at cost      240,000    Total liabilities          248,000
  Less accumulated
    depreciation                 (138,000)   EQUITY
  Net equipment                   102,000    Net assets                 308,000
Total assets                      556,000    Total liabilities
                                               and equity               556,000

Find your inventory. Medical equipment is carried at $240,000 of original cost with $138,000 of accumulated depreciation against it, so its net book value is $102,000. That $102,000 is not what the equipment is worth, not what it would cost to replace, and not a statement about how much life it has left. It is cost minus the depreciation taken so far, and nothing else.

The income statement for the same year

Net patient service revenue                                       742,000
Other operating revenue                                            18,000
Total operating revenue                                           760,000

Salaries, wages and benefits                                      418,000
Supplies and drugs                                                152,000
Purchased services and maintenance                                 64,000
Depreciation and amortization                                      41,000
Interest                                                            9,000
Other operating expenses                                           58,000
Total operating expenses                                          742,000

Operating income                                                   18,000

Three lines on this statement are yours. Salaries and benefits carries your staff. Purchased services and maintenance carries your contracts and vendor labor. Depreciation carries the capital items you asked for in previous years, which is the quiet reason a capital committee is cautious: every approval it grants becomes an expense line on this statement for a decade.

Depreciation and book value, worked

A $1,000,000 system, ten-year useful life, no salvage value
Annual depreciation      (1,000,000 - 0) / 10                100,000 per year
End of year 1 book value 1,000,000 - 100,000                   900,000
End of year 3 book value 1,000,000 - 300,000                   700,000
End of year 10 book      1,000,000 - 1,000,000                       0
value
Disposed in year 7       remaining book value written off       300,000

The year-seven line is the one that reaches a manager. Replacing that system in year seven costs the hospital the new purchase plus a $300,000 write-off of remaining book value, and finance must agree to the write-off before the old asset moves. A fully depreciated device in year eleven, by contrast, can be disposed of with no write-off at all, which is occasionally the cheapest year to replace something.

What to memorize

Balance sheet       one day; assets = liabilities + equity
Income statement    a period; revenue - expenses = net income
Cash flow           cash in and out; profit is not cash
Straight-line       (cost - salvage) / useful life, per year
Book value          cost - accumulated depreciation
Fully depreciated   book value zero; says nothing about condition or life
Payable/receivable  owed to vendors / owed to the hospital
